SM22L-A1.free_elimination: None truly free. -12 is the c that makes k=-6 coincident (infinitely many), a natural trap rather than a free strike. No range/sign/closure tell; plugging c back requires the whole parallel-lines analysis for both k=6 and k=-6.
SM22L-A1.note: No solution needs k^2=36. k=6 must NOT give no-solution, so k=6 must give coincident lines: 6x+3y=18 -> 12x+6y=36, c=36. Then k=-6: 12x-6y=-12 vs 12x-6y=36, parallel distinct. Decision point (making the positive k coincident) is genuine.

SM22L-A2.free_elimination: Plug-back is fast and decisive: k=7 gives x<3 (largest integer 2, fails), k=8 gives x<3.2 (largest integer 3). Since the stem asks for the SMALLEST k, testing options in ascending order finds the key on the second try without deriving 7<k<=12. Two adjacent pairs (7,8) and (11,12) so no lone-pair adjacency tell. Nothing struck for free without plugging.
SM22L-A2.note: x<(8+k)/5; need 3<(8+k)/5<=4 -> 7<k<=12; smallest integer 8. Boundary strictness is the intended decision but ascending plug-in bypasses it.

SM22L-A3.free_elimination: Options are the four combinations of slope +/-2/3 and +/-3/2 (sign pairs and reciprocal pairs). A student who sees that 'shift left = shift down' means a decreasing line knows the x-intercept of a decreasing line through (3,7) is > 3, striking -15/2 and -5/3 - but that sign reasoning is half the item's real work, so not counted as free. Remaining decision 6/4 vs 4/6 is the actual insight.

SM22L-A4.free_elimination: None. No closure or range tell; options are all plausible fees.
SM22L-A4.note: A(30)=90, A(70)=150, slope 1.5, F=90-45=45. The input shift is a decision but once parsed it is two-point linear arithmetic.

SM22L-A6.note: Overlap needs 3x-7<c-2x -> x<(c+7)/5; need (c+7)/5<=4 -> c<=13. At c=13 x<4 strictly so x=4 excluded. Desmos with a slider can find it.
